title: How To Be More Consistent Next School Year
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin offers a simple, concrete ten-minute exercise meant to be done over the summer to build the consistency needed for firm rule enforcement the following year. The technique: draw a rectangle in the center of a page, list your classroom rules inside it, then write every misbehavior witnessed the previous year outside the rectangle, and finally draw a line connecting each misbehavior to the specific rule it breaks. His central claim is that this exercise serves two purposes — first, it stress-tests whether your existing rules actually cover every misbehavior you're likely to encounter, revealing gaps that need a new rule if a line can't be clearly drawn; second, reviewing the completed diagram builds the instant certainty a teacher needs to enforce consequences without hesitation, uncertainty, or fear once the new year begins. He notes the exercise is one he's described before but considers worth repeating because of its effectiveness, and adds that high school teachers will typically need more rules and a different consequence system to achieve the same coverage.
points: The exercise: box your rules, list last year's misbehaviors outside the box, then draw a line from each misbehavior to the rule it breaks.
Any misbehavior that can't be clearly linked to a rule reveals a gap that needs a new rule before the next school year.
Reviewing the completed diagram is said to build the instant certainty needed to enforce consequences without hesitation.
High school teachers will typically need considerably more rules and a different consequence system to achieve the same coverage.
